en: A Direct Explanation of the *Ālambanaparīkṣāvṛtti* (Commentary on the Treatise Examining the Object of Cognition) Composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
The Commentary composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing.
Lüyi’s Commentary:

Zhixu explains that if one says [this teaching] can enable those with poisonous wisdom to become wise, it is for the sake of making their insight extremely clear and for the purpose of eliminating evil deeds.
Having paid homage with reverence, one should contemplate its meaning.

This is the homage by which the intent of this commentary is set forth. As for the term "if one speaks," it refers to the words and language of the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* (Treatise on Examining the Object-Condition).
Words are the Teaching (*dharma*); examination is Practice (*pratipatti*); and the object-condition is the Principle (*naya*).
These Three Jewels were originally spoken only by the Buddha; Dignāga composed this treatise to elucidate them. This is the Bodhi... [text continues].
"Saṃgha. Thus, in this single word and character, the three virtues and the Three Jewels are all fully present. Regarding "poisonous wisdom":
the non-Buddhists' dualistic attachments to a self and to dharmas are the poisons of view and affliction; the attachment to dharmas in the remaining vehicles is the poison of ignorance.
Because they are associated with these poisons, they are called "poisonous wisdom. Due to this poisonous wisdom, it causes ordinary beings and non-Buddhists to give rise to outflows (*āsrava*).

The evil of [denying] this [reality] invites the fruit of *paricchinna-vedanīya* (segmented existence) and causes other vehicles to stagnate in the evil of partial emptiness, serving as the cause for *pariṇāma-vipāka* (transformational existence).

Now, this *Ālambana-parīkṣā* (Treatise on the Investigation of the Object of Cognition) negates the non-existence of external objects while demonstrating that the aspectual division (*nimitta-bhāga*) is not non-existent;

it refutes the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) to reveal the *paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) natures, and elucidates *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only) to manifest the Middle Way. It is able to [neutralize] the poison...
Wisdom, when realized in the present moment, immediately becomes the most lucid insight. Once insight is lucid, evil naturally vanishes.

This treatise thus accords with the Buddha’s intent above and benefits all sentient beings below in this manner; therefore, having prostrated in reverence, I shall once again contemplate its meaning and provide this commentary.

Below this, I shall provide an explanation of the text. It is necessary to cite the original treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), and thus I have used the text of that treatise itself as the topical outline (*vibhāga*).

I do not dare to establish further elaborate outlines. Since I am borrowing the text of the treatise to serve as the outline, I have written it indented by two characters to facilitate reading and comprehension.
May the Bodhisattvas, in their great compassion, surely forgive my transgression.
Treatise: Regarding those who maintain that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, take external forms as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the treatise says:

Those who assert the existence of visual and other consciousnesses [must admit] that with respect to objects that are discarded or objects that are gathered, there is either relinquishing or grasping.
This is because it observes the fruit; the entities that are abandoned and the causes of inversion are what are revealed here.

This generally clarifies the main points of the externalist attachments previously recounted. The treatise says: "Regarding those who assert that there are consciousnesses such as visual consciousness..."
This restates the treatise's argument. Below the phrase "that which is discarded," its meaning is then explained.

"That which is discarded" refers to the two phenomena—the atoms and their aggregation—maintained by the externalist; these are definitively non-existent, and therefore the Mahāyāna refutes and discards them.

Regarding the "matter to be included": this refers to the two terms accepted by the opponent—namely, "the arising of consciousness" and "bearing an aspect"—which are not erroneous with respect to their meaning;

therefore, even if the Mahāyāna were to provisionally accept them, it would include them. In this way, by abandoning the matter to be discarded and taking up the matter to be included, one achieves the result of the thesis-property (*pakṣadharma*) established through the reason (*hetu*); only then can it be called a true refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). Within this context...

This treatise reveals the abandonment of the two types of objective entities—the external atoms and their aggregation—as well as the causes of error consisting in the deficiency of either one of these factors.
By revealing those causes of error, one is able to refute the conceived entities of atoms and their aggregation;
through the refutation of the conceived atoms and their aggregation, [the selflessness of phenomena is established].
Since it cannot function as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), one can thereby demonstrate the fundamental tenet that there are no phenomena external to the mind.
Therefore, in order to set forth the correct meaning and establish a valid proof, one must first refute the externalist attachments.

In this context, the word "etc. (ādi) refers to the five types of consciousness that depend upon the physical sense faculties as accepted by others. This is because others maintain that these [five] invariably take real entities (*dravya*) as their objects.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not like this, as it is not invariably so; for it is accepted that, conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), it takes things such as chariots as its objects.
Even if one were to grant that the mental consciousness has a partial capacity to take real entities as its objects, it is still capable of taking [such objects].
Since there is no object separate from its corresponding aspect, once it is established that the object is not separate from the visual consciousness and so forth, [the argument] is then proven;
therefore, no further effort is required here.

This refers to the word "equal" (*sama*) in this treatise, which encompasses the five types of consciousness that depend upon the five pure material faculties (*pañca-rūpa-prasāda-indriya*), as commonly accepted by other vehicles.

Question: Why is the investigation of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) discussed only with respect to the first five consciousnesses and not with respect to the sixth consciousness? Answer: Because, according to other vehicles, regarding those five consciousnesses—[one...]

This is because [the opponent] previously maintained that the objects of the mind are real entities existing external to the cognizing consciousness; therefore, it must be refuted. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not like this, as it is not invariably so.
Other vehicles also admit that the mental consciousness takes conventionally existent things as its objects, since it can take various provisional phenomena such as chariots as its objects.
Even if one were to grant, for the sake of argument, that there is some portion of the mental consciousness taking real entities as its objects, [it would still be incorrect].
Furthermore, one can demonstrate that even for the independent *manovijñāna*, its appearance—which resembles [the object]—is not separated from what it grasps as an external object.

Now, regarding the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, it must first be established through reasoning that their objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is certainly not separable from the object;
only then will it be properly established. Therefore, this should not be applied to the *manovijñāna*.
"Expediently" means that there is no need for detailed analysis.
Furthermore, the forms understood by the wisdom resulting from habitual cultivation are truly not the domain of *taṭhāgata* (here translated as "sentient conceptualization").
Furthermore, because it is established according to what is perceived, this [consciousness] now observes only the objects of the wisdoms born of hearing, reflection, and innate attainment.
Thus, the objects apprehended by this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are entirely non-existent, as it cannot apprehend its own constituent aggregates.

Furthermore, because past and future objects are not real entities, they are like unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). For this reason, these terms include the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).

Fearing that someone might ask: "If you claim that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not take real entities as its objects, then how can the wisdom resulting from habitual cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala-jñāna*) [function] regarding them?"...
Is not the form-dharma that is realized as the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) within dhyāna a sphere of objects known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? To explain this now:
Furthermore, the form realized by the wisdom that is the fruit of habitual cultivation is truly not a sphere traversed by conceptual construction, because it is established exactly as it is seen.
That is to say, having attained the wisdom that is the fruit of habitual cultivation, one naturally transcends [conceptualization].

Regarding the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), one must certainly not falsely imagine that the determinate fruit-form (*niyata-phala-rūpa*) is a real self or real phenomena external to the mind.

In this treatise, we consider only the objects of the wisdom acquired through hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom acquired through reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) as the objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
In this way, it is understood that the objects apprehended by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) during the state of distraction (*vikṣipta-avasthā*) are entirely non-existent.
There is. Because this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can by no means directly perceive the collection of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the five present sensory consciousnesses;
or because if it were to perceive the past or future, those would not be real entities, just as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not existent dharmas.
Therefore, the word "equal" (*sama*) in this treatise merely includes the first five bodies of consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*) and does not necessarily include [the mental consciousness].
Regarding mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*): if that is so, how is it that all mental consciousnesses are induced by the sense-consciousnesses?
This question is posed because of what was stated in the preceding text—that this [mental consciousness] cannot take its own aggregate as an object. That is to say:
If it is claimed that the mental consciousness cannot take the fivefold collection of colors as its object,
then how could the mental consciousness induced by the five sense-consciousnesses not likewise take the five sensory objects as its objects?

It is not the case that this [mental consciousness] arises simultaneously with its root-consciousness (indriya-vijñāna), nor does it arise immediately after it, because it takes form and other objects as its objective support (*ālambana*).

Alternatively, it takes the present as its object; however, this is not something previously apprehended by the root-consciousness. Thus, the mental consciousness itself is able to directly perceive the essential nature of external objects.

If this were so, it would follow that there would be no such things as the deaf or the blind, which would further contradict the inferential knowledge that there exists a distinct [mental consciousness].
[Question]: Regarding the faculties. [Answer]: It is not the case that this induced mental consciousness arises simultaneously with the five preceding sensory consciousnesses.

Since it is called "induced," there must necessarily be a sequence of priority and posteriority. Furthermore, this mental consciousness [arises] either from those that have just ceased without interval, or...
Because visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles serve as objects of cognition, these five sensory objects (pañca-viṣaya) are merely manifestations of the mind.

Arising at the very moment of birth, they perish immediately and cannot remain for even an instant; thus, they induce the arising of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which can only take as its object the shadows of those [objects] that have already passed away, rather than the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of them.
Furthermore, one might fear the following objection: "Is it not granted that the simultaneous mental consciousness takes the external five [sensory objects] as its objects?"
[Objection: Is it not a fault? [Response: Now, the explanation is given as follows: It may be granted that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes a present object as its condition.
However, since this mental consciousness arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, it cannot take as its object that which was previously apprehended by the sense-consciousnesses.

Even if one grants that the mental consciousness takes those five objects as its conditions, this would mean that the mental consciousness itself could directly perceive the essential nature of external objects; [but this is not the case].
If one were to rely on the five sensory consciousnesses [of the preceding moments], this would result in the absence of deafness, blindness, and so forth;

furthermore, it would contradict the inference that there is a distinct function for the five physical sense organs. This clearly demonstrates that the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) also cognizes by means of its own transformed images;

there is absolutely no principle whereby it could directly perceive external objects. If one were to grant that the mental consciousness can directly perceive objects, then those who are deaf or blind...
There is also mental consciousness; why then can it alone not take sound and form as its objects?

Furthermore, if mental consciousness is already capable of cognizing external objects by itself, then the function of the five sense organs in producing consciousness would likewise be rendered useless.

This excludes the increase of form (*rūpa*), as that is what is intended. However, no further consideration is given to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because the visual and other sensory consciousnesses exist only by having form as their objective support and condition.
Furthermore, since non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is of the nature of mere non-action, it is admitted by [the opponent] himself to be non-existent.
This is the intended meaning.
"Added color" (*adhika-rūpa*) refers to the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) external to the mind as they are grasped [by other schools].

The reason this treatise merely negates "added color" is that it is precisely what other vehicles (non-Buddhist systems) desire; therefore, it must be specifically refuted to clarify that there is no external object-condition (*bāhya-ālambana-pratyaya*).
It does not exist. Nevertheless, one should no longer harbor doubts regarding mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

This is because the five sensory consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, necessarily depend upon the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) as their basis and take material objects (*rūpaviṣaya*) as their conditions before they can arise.

As for the unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*) that serves as the object of mental consciousness, it is admitted by [the Vaibhāṣikas] themselves to be non-existent, precisely because its nature is that of non-action; it is not like the external five objects of the senses as they are imagined [by others].
The original intent was thus; therefore, it is unnecessary to analyze this in terms of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

This [consciousness], with respect to its object (*ālambana*), is about to be treated as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is of the nature of that which is apprehended (*grāhya*). Because it has deeply entered a wrong path, the primary intention here is to negate its status as an object;
by way of this incidental discussion, one then negates its status as a support (*āśraya*). As for the function of the simultaneous sense organ (*indriya*):
...of color. This intends to set forth a refutation of their desire to increase the [number of] colors. There are two kinds of external colors added to the mind as they maintain:
first, the color of the supporting sense-faculties (*indriya-rūpa*); second, the color of the perceived objects (*viṣaya-rūpa*). Now, first—

Regarding the refutation of the object of cognition: because such individuals falsely take their objects of cognition to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), believing they have truly attained external objects and developing deep attachment to them, they tread upon a false path; this is particularly lamentable.

For this reason, the primary intent here is merely to refute and dismantle that false calculation of the five consciousnesses’ objects as being the nature of a composite of atoms. [This continues] until...
In the subsequent passage, the nature of the sense-faculties upon which these five consciousnesses rely is further refuted as a matter of course.
Here, regarding the functional form (rūpa) of the simultaneous faculty, the author provisionally employs the character "she" (設) to grant it for the sake of argument.
Regarding the term "external object" (*bāhyārtha*): they [the opponents] maintain that there exists a distinct object apart from this [consciousness]. This [term] reveals their error.
It is called an "object" because it reveals their adherence to the existence of a separate entity that can be apprehended.
Regarding "external objects": this refers to the two characters "external form" (*bāhya-rūpa*) found in the treatise.
Fearing that there might be an objection stating, "If external objects do not exist, why does the treatise itself speak of 'external form'?", the present commentary explains:

The term "external objects" is used because those of other vehicles falsely cling to the notion that there are distinct objects separate from these five consciousnesses. This is intended precisely to reveal their error; therefore, it is not truly external.

It is designated as "external" by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Furthermore, it is shown that there is a false attachment to the existence of a distinct entity that could be apprehended;
thus, although it is not an actual object, it is metaphorically called an "object.
How, then, could one say it is a "total aggregate"? Since it is not a total aggregate, it is logically consistent for it to be a real entity (*dravya*).
"Aggregate" (*saṃcita*) refers to what is called "conjunction" (*sāmagrī*) later in the treatise;
"substantial entity" (*dravya*) refers to what is called the "atom" (*paramāṇu*) later in the treatise. Question: Since external objects do not exist, how can one speak of an "aggregate"?
If it is not the case that the aggregate is refuted as being without reality, then would it not follow that the atom as a substantial entity accords with correct reasoning?
Truly, as you have said, it is difficult to refute. Since that [position] itself contradicts its own internal logic from beginning to end, what further fault could there be for me?

Because it is accepted that [cognition] takes both real entities and their collective aggregates as its objects, I shall set aside this particular objection for now in order to set forth its other specific faults.

The answer is: Truly, as you have challenged me, the fault still lies with him; what loss is there for me? For if he maintains that it is a "total collection" (samudāya), it contradicts the principle of the syllables (*akṣara*) as conditions.

If he maintains that it is a "real entity" (*dravya*), it contradicts the principle of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Therefore, it is said that the principles of the preceding and succeeding [arguments] are mutually contradictory.
Alternatively, one might take the real entity as the object-condition, or one might take the total collection as [the object-condition].
Since the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is merely what they falsely assert, the Mahāyāna school now intends to set forth its distinct faults regarding the deficiency of two factors;
thus, it shall for the moment let pass the fault of their false calculation that atoms are real. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"If even the assertion that atoms exist leads to such a fallacy, how much more so when there is no consciousness?"
The external, real atom (*paramāṇu*) is precisely what is intended here.
The treatise states: "Some maintain that atoms exist as substantial entities because they are capable of producing consciousness;
others allow for atoms, asserting that although they are merely atoms that arise and cease only when aggregated together, they nonetheless possess substantial reality."
Each [sense faculty] takes its respective object individually; it does not take a composite aggregate as its object, just like the case of visible forms and so forth.

Even if all of one's own sense faculties were to be present simultaneously, their objects would not be confused, because the functional capacity of each faculty is determined by its own specific nature, and thus they possess the ability to discern and differentiate actual entities.

Each individual atom constitutes an objective referent (*ālambana-viṣaya*), because it serves as their causal nature; that is, because it serves as the causal nature for those consciousnesses of the eye and so forth.
This means it is the direct and proximate factor for their arising. However, some say that the objective referent is the cause for the arising of consciousness.
Because of these various conditions, this detailed exposition of the false proof regarding atoms serves as the basis for the true refutation to follow.
It says that some may falsely assert that atoms function as objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*); this is because, although they are...

When atoms aggregate together, arising and ceasing are perceived; however, the five consciousnesses each take these atoms as their substantial entities as their respective objects, rather than taking the provisional phenomenon of a combined aggregate as its object.

This is just like the five sense-objects—form, sound, odor, taste, and touch—which, even when all the corresponding faculties are present before them, do not become confused with one another within the spheres of those five objects.
Because the functions of those five faculties are each determined, with respect to the substantial entities of the atoms,
the eye perceives color, the ear perceives sound, the nose perceives fragrance, the tongue perceives flavor, and the body perceives tangibility.

It is called "the capacity for cutting off" (the continuum of existence). Therefore, one should know that each individual atom constitutes the objective field (*ālambana*) of the five consciousnesses.

Furthermore, because it is the causal nature of those five consciousnesses, it is also termed an "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*). For this reason, they are collectively designated as the "object-condition.
Why is this? It is because these atoms are the cause of those five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth.
Because it is their nature, it constitutes the meaning of being the "friend-like portion" for the arising of those five consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness and the rest.
However, some say that the objective referent (*ālambana*) itself is the cause for the arising of consciousness, because it is included among the various conditions (*pratyaya*).

Regarding the meaning of the "friend-like portion," this means that the direct causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) are like parents, while the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is like a friend.
The various conditions are the four conditions: first, the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); second, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);

third, the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); and fourth, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Herein, the formal argument is as follows: "An atom is the subject; it is established that it is an objective condition, because it possesses the nature of being a cause.
However, there is no similar example (*sapakṣa*).
Treatise: Some maintain that it is the "conjunction" (saṃghāta), because when consciousness arises, it bears the aspect of that [conjunction].

Others, regarding it as a "total aggregate" (piṇḍa), hold that the conjunction of all those atoms is the objective support (ālambana) for this [consciousness], because consciousness arises bearing the aspect of that.
Since cognition is produced based on a total aggregate, it is therefore known with certainty that...
That serves as the objective referent (*ālambana*). As it has been said: "If consciousness possesses the aspect (*ākāra*) of that [object], then that is its object.
This is a detailed exposition of the false attachment to a semblance of a logical reason (*sādhanābhāsa*) through synthesis, which serves as the basis for the true refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
As for the statement that one might instead apprehend the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) as a composite whole:
that [position] holds that the collection of all the atoms (*paramāṇu*) is the object-condition of these five consciousnesses, because consciousness arises in the form of a composite whole.
Since the cognition of discernment (*vijñapti-jñāna*) arises from the composite whole, it is certain that—
That [collection] is taken as a collective whole to serve as the object of cognition (*ālambana*). As it has been said: "If consciousness possesses a certain aspect, that [aspect] is its object.
Now, since the aspect of a collective whole exists within the five sensory consciousnesses, how could that collective whole not be the object of these five consciousnesses?
Regarding this, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The collection is the subject (*dharmin*); it is the object of consciousness...
Regarding the thesis: the reason given is "because consciousness arises from its object. Furthermore, there is no similar example (*sapakṣa*).
[The opponent] argues: Both [positions] are unreasonable. Why?
Because both proponents of these two theories maintain that their respective positions accord with this principle.
It is still said that one considers oneself to be in accord with principle; this concludes the description of their deluded conceptualization.

If the reason is not stated, this reason lacks an example. It is like establishing that the nature of the atoms as a whole is the objective referent (*ālambana*) by means of the reason of being the nature of atoms and so forth.
Generally speaking, the principles for establishing a formal argument are as follows: the preceding term is the qualified (viśeṣya), while the succeeding term is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa).

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is to be established, and the reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes it. The reason is that which is to be conjoined, and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is that which effects the conjunction.
Now, although those two treatises each present a reason, they ultimately lack a concordant example; this makes them appear as if no reason had ever been stated at all. Since these two reasons...
In all cases there is no analogy; it is simply that by means of causes, the nature of causality is established, and by means of a thesis, the nature of being a thesis is established.
This is because they establish it on the basis of the two types—the ultimate atom and the general characteristic—as being the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana*).
Since there is no example to support the reason (*hetu*), there is consequently no reason to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*). Therefore, both [positions] are irrational.

Furthermore, if you yourself admit that one does not apprehend a real entity external to consciousness, there would necessarily be the fallacy of contradicting the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*).
However, Dharmakīrti does not accept this; rather, he takes what is commonly accepted even by others as his own analogy.
If it were merely as stated, it would have to apply to the thesis (*sādhya*) itself.

The intention of the previous formal argument (*prayoga*) was that the two reasons (*hetu*) in the root treatise merely clarify the grounds for the reason and are not the reasons themselves, because there was no commonly established analogy. For this reason, it was necessary to set forth those [analogies].
Why is it that the corresponding cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is as it is? Furthermore, this next section demonstrates that the principles discussed by [the author] himself are free from error.

Question: Why does the Mahāyāna not immediately establish its own correct measure (*pramāṇa*), but instead first concedes that each of the two treatises possesses one branch [of argument] before subsequently refuting them?
Explanation: Moreover, if one has not yet refuted their adherence to the combination of atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta*), [the refutation cannot proceed].

Both [positions] are irrational. If one first admits that the internal *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of form (*rūpa*) serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness, rather than consciousness taking an external actual entity as its object, then there arises the doubt that an actual entity originally exists outside of consciousness;

yet, since the five consciousnesses do not go out to apprehend it, there would be the fault of contradicting the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an existing phenomenon. Furthermore, regarding the form-dharma of the *nimitta-bhāga*, the rest...
All [other] vehicles likewise reject this; that is to say, it is an instance of "the qualified object being unestablished" (*asiddha-viśeṣya*) for one party among the opponents.

Therefore, setting aside for the moment those doctrines accepted by our own school, we shall take as our illustration only those things accepted as common even by the other [schools], namely the sense faculties and the two moons. If it were merely as the other vehicles maintain...

By stating the reason (*hetu*), one establishes the similar example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*), which must correspond to the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established, so that they are sequentially connected and the property (*dharma*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are mutually congruent; thus, one may refute their false attachments.

Furthermore, the reason for first recounting the prior arguments of other vehicles is that, although their fundamental treatises contain both the theory of consciousness arising with images (*sākāra-vijñāna*) and the theory of consciousness arising without images (*nirākāra-vijñāna*), [the author intends to address them].
This is a "reason" (*hetu*) only in the sense of clarifying why [the reason] is a reason; it is not the "reason" among the three members [of a syllogism].
This is because, lacking a commonly established example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it does not constitute a valid reason. For this purpose, one must state a reason that corresponds to the opponent's own tenets.
Why is it that each lacks a similar example? Why is it that they mutually lack one member? Thus, they are already fallacious means of cognition (*tarka*).
Refutation. Furthermore, [the author] demonstrates that the principle he has argued is free from error and is truly a valid proof (*sādhana*).

Treatise: Regarding the atom (*paramāṇu*) in relation to the five consciousnesses, even if it serves as a condition, it is not an object-condition (*ālambana*), because its form does not appear to consciousness, just like the eye faculty and so forth.

This establishes that it is accepted by others; thus, the fifth case is employed. Even if it were granted as a reason (*hetu*), it would be like those things commonly accepted as non-existent, because of their lack of existence.
This first explains the meaning of the word "even if" (*cet*) in the verse. The "fifth case" refers to the fifth among the eight grammatical cases (*vibhakti*).
The five characteristics are termed "following from" (*anvaya*) in the sense of being derived from [the opponent's] position; this is a term used for granting a concession, not an actual admission.

It is just as when worldly people collectively accept things such as the hair of a tortoise, the horns of a rabbit, or the son of a barren woman—all of which are non-existent entities—precisely because they lack the nature of existence.

It is not because atoms are the cause; moreover, even if one were to grant that the essence of atoms constitutes their causal nature, it is only said that they do not possess the nature of being an object of cognition (*ālambana*), because they lack the characteristics of an atom as defined by its [perceptual] aspect.
This is why it is said that for the sensory consciousnesses (*indriya-vijñāna*), atoms are not the objective domain.
This is the correct explanation of the thesis and the reason. Regarding the statement that the five consciousnesses arise, in reality they do not have atoms (*paramāṇu*) as their cause.

Furthermore, even if one were to grant that the substance of the various atoms is a real entity (*dravyadharma*) and could thus function as a causal factor, it would still be incorrect to say they possess the nature of being an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
This is because they do not possess the characteristics of what is perceived by those five consciousnesses; rather, they still possess the characteristics of atoms themselves. Therefore...
This refutation states: The consciousnesses produced by the five sense-faculties do not have those ultimate atoms as their objective referents (*ālambana*).
As for the claim that they are "like the faculties," this means that although the faculties are indeed the direct causal basis for consciousness, they lack the characteristics of an object.
It is not the object-domain of those [consciousnesses]. The same applies to atoms (*paramāṇu*).

This explanation serves as a concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*): for instance, although the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are the direct supporting causes (*sākṣād-āśraya-hetu*) of the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), the characteristics of the five faculties do not exist within the five consciousnesses;
they are not the objects of perception (*ālambana-viṣaya*) of those five consciousnesses. Atoms are likewise: although...
Even that which is admitted to exist substantially is not an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
What is meant by the statement: "That which lacks its characteristic is not the domain of this"? It is for this reason that it is called the "domain of the name" (*nāmaviṣaya*), and so forth.

This is the response that resolves the objection. The question asks: "If it is the case that those [objects] which lack characteristics are not the objective spheres (*ālambana*) of this consciousness, then what is meant when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the past, future, and so forth as its objects?
The answer states: "It is for this reason that one speaks of 'name-spheres' (*nāmaviṣaya*) and the like.

That is to say, that which possesses a substantial basis (*dravya*) upon which one can rely is called an "objective sphere of things" (*vastuviṣaya*); that which lacks a substantial basis upon which one can rely is... [a name-sphere].
The "named object" (*nāma-viṣaya*) refers to names; the "substantial object" (*vastu-viṣaya*) pertains to all six consciousnesses, whereas the named object exists only in the sixth consciousness.

Treatise: Regarding the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it means that the perceiving consciousness arises bearing the aspect (*ākāra*) of that [object], and that there is a real entity which causes the perceiving consciousness to arise by relying upon it.
Regarding the term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): it refers to the ascertainment (*niścaya*) that apprehends specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
How, then, is this further designated as "apprehension"? It is because consciousness arises in the likeness of those [objects'] aspects.

The intended meaning of this statement is that consciousness arises with the same appearance as those [objects], and by conforming to their essence, it is said to "apprehend that object. However, in reality, there is no separate object of apprehension apart from consciousness itself.
"Self-nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to what is called the "substantial entity" (*dravya*) in the verse; it is that which serves as the condition for the arising of consciousness.

"Apprehended" (*vijñāta*) refers to what is called "arising with the aspect of that" in the verse; this means that the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is apprehended by the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*), and is therefore termed the "object-condition" (*ālambana*).

Regarding "specific and general characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): that which is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), apart from names, conceptual seeds, and so forth, is called the "specific" (*sva*).

The "characteristic" (nimitta) refers to that which evolves in dependence upon conventional cognition (*prajñapti*) and its designations; it is called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), and it is precisely the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
"Ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*) means to discern with certainty and clarity; it is the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*). Question:

How can these self-characteristics and common characteristics also be termed "ascertainment"? Answer: Because the consciousness of discernment arises in accordance with those self-characteristics and common characteristics.
Therefore, the intended meaning of this statement is that consciousness arises in a manner identical to the essential nature and appearance of its object.
Because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) transforms into the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) in accordance with the substance of that essential nature, it is said to "cognize" that object.
In reality, however, there is no separate object of cognition apart from one's own consciousness.

Could it be that consciousness acts as the causal nature [of the object]? However, there is merely the appearance of the preceding object, which is projected within itself like a reflection in a mirror;
it is commonly agreed that this is what constitutes the cognition of that object.

This question and answer resolve a doubt. The question asks: "If that which is cognized is not identical to the objective essence, then can this objective essence serve as the causal nature for its cognition? The answer says:
"However, there is merely the appearance of the preceding object, which is projected upon its own cognition like a reflection in a mirror; this is what is commonly accepted [as the object]."

For its object, this [condition] possesses both the meanings of "carrying" (*sahagata*) and "producing consciousness" (*vijñānotpādaka*); therefore, it can function as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

Treatise: Although atoms (*paramāṇu*) such as form (*rūpa*) may possess substantial reality and be capable of producing the five consciousnesses, they might still be considered objects in that sense. However...

It is not an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just as the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and so forth are not; for within the visual consciousness and the others, the characteristic of those [faculties] does not exist.
Likewise, atoms (*paramāṇu*) lack the status of being objects of cognition for the visual consciousness and the others.
However, it is not the case that consciousness conforms to the individual self-natures of each atom such that these atoms constitute the objective entity (*ālambana-vastu*).

Even if they possess the nature of being causes, they are not objects of cognition in the sense of being causal factors; just as the sense organs, though possessing the nature of being causes, do not function as objects of cognition.

If it is admitted that [the object] acts as an objective support (ālambana) by virtue of being its cause, then the sense organs (indriya) would likewise be so, and thus they too should become that [objective support].

This is the correct explanation of the treatise’s argument. It states that the individual substance of each atom (paramāṇu) cannot be said to possess the characteristics corresponding to those [five consciousnesses].
Therefore, even if one were to grant that atoms serve as the substantial essence (svabhāva) of the objective field, this might still be the case.

Regarding the nature of being a cause: it is not the case that something becomes an object of cognition (*ālambana*) merely by virtue of having the status of a cause, as for example, the five sense faculties.

Although they possess the nature of being causes, they do not serve as objects for the five consciousnesses. If, however, one were to grant that something could be an object simply because it has the nature of being a cause, [it would lead to absurd consequences].
Then the five sense faculties would likewise be composed of such atoms, and they should consequently become the objects of apprehension for those five consciousnesses.
But how could such a principle possibly exist?

This statement refers to the previously mentioned reasoning regarding their correspondence; therefore, there is the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*). However, what is intended to be revealed is not merely this...
The causal nature is precisely the characteristic that serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*) for that consciousness.

If, as you have stated, this causal nature is intended to serve as the logical reason (*sādhana*), then is that causal nature itself the nature of the object-condition? Furthermore, regarding the sense faculties (*indriya*), there would also be the fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).
This is merely a clarification of the intent behind the provisional acceptance; it is not a genuine admission.

While the external atoms (*paramāṇu*) asserted by other vehicles are indeed erroneous, the statement that the substantial entity can serve as the cause for the arising of consciousness is still worth considering.
Since this accords with their own reasoning, we shall tentatively accept its causal status, though there remains the issue of the unestablished nature (*asiddha*) of the reason.
This is a fault regarding the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). However, the intended meaning is not that the nature of the cause itself is the objective condition;
rather, it negates its status as an objective condition. It does not actually grant that [the atom] can be established as the cause that produces consciousness.

If, as they claim, the atom were the cause that produces consciousness and were thus established as the probans (*sādhana*), then since that causal nature would already be established, [the argument would be redundant].
Could it not also be established that [atoms] possess the nature of being an object of cognition (*ālambana*)?

Furthermore, as for using the sense faculties (*indriya*) as a homologous example (*dṛṣṭānta*), this merely uses the fact that the sense faculties are not objects of cognition to illustrate that the atoms you assert are likewise not objects of cognition.

It does not establish that because the sense faculties can produce consciousness, those atoms—which you claim are effects—can likewise produce consciousness. Even if one were to actually grant that [the atoms exist],...
If atoms (*paramāṇu*) were taken as the cause, there would likewise be the fallacy of inconclusiveness regarding the analogy of the sense faculties (*indriya*). Why is this?
Atoms are falsely imagined by other vehicles and are thus termed "invalid cognition" (*apramāṇa*); the five sense faculties are accepted by the Mahāyāna and are thus termed "inference" (*anumāna*).
If one were to equate atoms with the five sense faculties, then atoms would likewise not be mere false conceptualizations;
yet if one were to equate the five sense faculties with atoms, then the five sense faculties would also become invalid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*). How could this possibly be acceptable?
If this is so, what is the meaning of the phrase "because it does not possess those characteristics"? It is intended to clarify the establishment of one's own position;
for one's own doctrine is not established merely by stating the faults of another's position.

This statement is made to demonstrate that [the object] is not itself the characteristic capable of producing its own cognition, and thus the object is not composed of atoms, just like the eye and other sense organs. If the phrase "if it were of the nature of their cause" [is used],...

The proponent intends to first establish the opponent's own position in order to clarify what is commonly accepted by both parties; at this stage, the purpose is to refute the opponent and manifest one's own view so that the meaning of the refutation may be established.
These words are placed here to determine the opponent's own tenet, rather than to establish an uncertain alternative position, for fear that the opponent might not accept it.
The following two rounds of question and answer both serve to clarify the principles of refutation and establishment. Now, the first round asks:

"If this is so, why do you not directly refute [the opponent] by stating that there are no atoms existing separately from the mind, but instead say only 'because they do not possess those characteristics'?
What is the meaning of this? The answer says: "It is for the purpose of clarifying the establishment of our own [position]."
The tenet that "there are no phenomena external to one's own mind" is established not merely by describing the faults of other schools' assertions regarding phenomena external to the mind;

rather, even if the Mahāyāna were to refrain from establishing formal syllogisms (*pramāṇa*) through the methods of affirmation and negation, it would nonetheless exhaust the reasoning and deplete the arguments of those other vehicles.
If one were to merely negate the atoms (*paramāṇu*) they cling to, then they would likewise have to negate the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) that I have established.

[The atoms] are divided into colors. Therefore, the present statement merely serves to exclude the notion that [atoms] can directly produce the objective aspect (*nimitta*) of their own consciousness;
it clarifies that the perceived object (*ālambana*) is not composed of ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), just as the eyes and other sense organs are not the [direct] objects of perception.

If one were to grant the claim that they possess the nature of being its cause, this would merely serve as a provisional presentation of another's position by the author of the treatise, rather than an actual establishment [of his own view].
This is merely a provisional concession made to clarify what is mutually accepted by both parties.

At this stage, the intent is to refute the opponent's view regarding the object of cognition (*ālambana*), so that one’s own position may subsequently be revealed as correct. This is done to ensure that the meaning of the refutation can be established;
therefore, these words of provisional concession are employed. Generally, the method for establishing a thesis (*pakṣa*) requires first making a partial concession in order to settle the matter.
He [the opponent] argues: "If one were to present an indeterminate reason (*anaikāntika*) against the opponent's thesis as a whole, I fear they would likewise not accept it for me.
Since presenting an indeterminate reason to the opponent constitutes a valid refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), why bother to further formulate an inference (*anumāna*) based on my own position?"

Generally speaking, what is called "indeterminate" does not necessarily mean it is definitively unestablished; rather, one fears it may lead to doubt. For this reason, it is necessary to further establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*).
Alternatively, that which is not characterized by those [specific] marks may lack a determinate nature regarding the various atoms (*paramāṇu*), just as when consciousness arises from marks.

This is called "ascertainment" (*niścaya*). Since that [object] is not [ascertained], it is clearly known that there is no basis for ascertaining this [consciousness] either; one should say it is because it lacks the nature of being ascertained.
Thus, the mere emergence of this cause is not an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just like the atoms of the sense faculties (*indriya-paramāṇu*).

This is the second round of question and answer. The question asks: "If this is so, then the previous instance of presenting an 'inconclusive' (*anaikāntika*) reason to the opponent was itself a valid refutation.
Why, then, is it necessary to further set forth an inference (*anumāna*) based on one's own school (*svasiddhānta*) in the subsequent text? The answer states:

"Generally speaking, when one says a reason is 'inconclusive,' it does not necessarily mean that the proof is definitively unsuccessful; rather, it is intended to cause doubt. For this reason, it is necessary to establish [the argument] once more."

This is the proof (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, it may be argued that these atoms (*paramāṇu*) are not the objective aspect (*ālambana-nimitta*) for the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, because the five consciousnesses lack the determinate capacity to discern individual atoms. This merely refutes the opponent;

next, [the author] further presents his own inference (*svatantra-anumāna*): "Consciousness must arise in accordance with the characteristics of its substantial object (*bhūta-rūpa*). This is what is meant.

It is definitively established. Since those five consciousnesses do not appear as having the characteristics of atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is clearly understood that there is no basis for [the claim] that they definitively apprehend [them].
Therefore, one should say that [atoms] lack the nature of definitive apprehension. For this reason, we shall now merely demonstrate that these atoms are not the objective condition (*ālambana*).
We provisionally employ the analogy of the sense faculties (*indriya*) to refute the position that atoms are not the objective condition. For now.
Even if one were to grant that there is the sense of "having an object," one must simply await the presentation of their own inference (*sva-pramāṇa*) in the subsequent text;

only then will it be definitively resolved. Furthermore, the claim that [consciousness] exists as having conditioned phenomena as its object will likewise collapse of its own accord without needing to be attacked.

Others further establish the distinctions between the various consciousnesses: "Eye-consciousness cannot cognize infinitesimal matter (*paramāṇu-rūpa*), because it lacks that characteristic, just like the consciousnesses of the other sense-faculties.
The same should be stated for the other consciousnesses by reversing this [argument]. This is as expressed by the term "sense-faculty" (*indriya*).
This indeed constitutes the vehicle (*yāna*). Its metaphor must be interpreted according to its specific meaning.
This passage describes how the Mahāyāna, with its remaining [arguments], refutes the externalist attachments as follows: The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is: Thesis:

Visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), as the subject (*dharmin*), cannot cognize infinitesimal matter (*paramāṇurūpa*). Reason: Because it lacks the appearance (*ākāra*) of that [matter]. Example: Like the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) and so forth.
Consciousness. ... up to the following syllogism: "Body-consciousness is a subject (dharmin) that cannot cognize the touch of atoms;

this is the thesis (pakṣa). The reason (hetu) is: 'because it lacks that characteristic. The example (dṛṣṭānta) is: 'like the consciousnesses of the eye-faculty and so forth. Therefore, it is said: 'so too for the other consciousnesses.

Conversely, one should state: 'this is like the word "faculty" (indriya). Indeed, these terms are mutually interchangeable and applicable, just as with the term 'vehicle' (yāna). This is the analogy."
This [distinction] must be understood by inferring the meaning from the specific context;
furthermore, even if the term "causal nature" were used, it would be redundant. Although that [object] functions as a cause, it does not possess the nature of being an object-condition (*ālambana*).
This case is likewise. It is indeed functional; however, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of sound and so forth cannot be the cause for the arising of consciousnesses belonging to other sense-faculties.

This precisely clarifies the inference (*anumāna*) established in the preceding passage. Although it appears to possess logical validity, there is a refutation (*bādha*) and no concession (*anugraha*); one must fear [the fallacy of over-extension].
One cannot definitively establish that thesis. Why is this? Suppose that person, based on this inference, were to shift their position and argue:
"Visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is the subject (*dharmin*); it definitely perceives the color-form of the aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃcita-rūpa*);

because it possesses that characteristic (*liṅga*), like other cognitions such as those of the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), etc. ... up to: "Tactile consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) is the subject; it definitely..."

[The opponent] is able to understand the thesis that the collection of atoms constitutes contact, on the grounds that "it possesses those characteristics," using as an analogy the consciousnesses of other sense organs, such as the eye.

Since I do not concede that those atoms can possess the nature of being a cause, they will further argue that the objects formed by the collection of atoms possess the nature of being an object of cognition (*ālambana*). Thus, this [argument of] Master Dignāga—though conceded...
The term "causal nature" would thus be rendered useless. How could one possibly silence the opponent by such means?
Now, the brilliance of Dignāga’s treatise lies in its clarification of what is commonly accepted by others; hence he says:

"Although those five sense-faculties possess causal efficacy, they do not have the nature of being objects of cognition (*ālambana*). These atoms are likewise so. Even if they were actually to possess causal efficacy, nevertheless..."

The atoms of sound cannot serve as the cause for the arising of visual, olfactory, or other such consciousnesses; the atoms of form cannot serve as the cause for the arising of auditory, olfactory, or other such consciousnesses;
and so on, up to the atoms of tangibility, which cannot serve as the cause for the arising of gustatory, olfactory, or other such consciousnesses.
Thus, even if one were to grant this point, half [of the opponent's position] would already be refuted. Why, then, must it be refuted entirely? This is because... [the beginning].
Even if one were to grant [the opponent's point] while implying a partial refutation, it would ultimately result in a complete refutation.
If, at the outset, there were a complete refutation, then regarding the meaning of ignorance as being commonly accepted by others, the opponent would likewise not accept my position.
Treatise: The collection [of atoms] is the object-condition for the five consciousnesses; even though it is not a [real] condition, its substance does not truly exist, just like a second moon.
Because the color-form and so forth that constitute the collection possess that appearance within visual consciousness and the others, they may indeed function as the object-condition.

However, there is no sense of an object-condition (*ālambana-artha*). Just as when the eyes are disordered one sees a second moon, which lacks substantial reality and is incapable of producing [cognition], so too this conjunction has no sense of an object-condition for visual consciousness and the other cognitions.
Some say that because the essence of consciousness does not manifest as an aggregate (the reason), it is not an object of cognition (the thesis), just like the sense organs (the example).
Since the arrangement of the characteristics of the object constitutes its nature as such, and this [aggregate] does not exist, it is logically stated that there is no manifestation as an aggregate.
Thus, for now, it has been explained that the *paramāṇu* (the ultimate atom) is not an object of cognition.

Because their proof (*sādhana*) is inconsistent, and because the nature of being an object (*viṣayatva*) is not well-established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If that is so, then the aggregate (*saṃcita*) is the object.

Thus, there are those of other vehicles who, having seen the Mahāyāna refute the position that atoms (*paramāṇu*) lack an objective referent (*ālambana*), subsequently formulate this counter-argument.
This statement is made based on their aggregation; however, because no accumulation appears within the very substance of consciousness itself, it is not its object of cognition (*ālambana*).
This is analogous to the atoms of the sense faculties. That the Mahāyāna refutes this is indeed reasonable. Why?

Because the arrangement of the objective characteristics within consciousness constitutes the nature of that which is the characteristic of the object of cognition; yet, consciousness does not [perceive] these atomic characteristics.
Because it exists, it is logically stated that there is no manifestation of an aggregate. Thus, for now, it has been shown that the atom (*paramāṇu*) is not the object-condition (*ālambana*).
This is because the proof (*sādhana*) of the first school is inconsistent, and because the Mahāyāna’s proof regarding the non-object-nature (*aviṣayatva*) is well-established.
If that is so, then the aggregate as a whole must be the object-condition of the five consciousnesses.
This is the object [of proof].

However, regarding all the probans (sādhana) that have been stated, if they are examined from the perspective of the Mūla school (namely, the Mahāyāna), they are all unestablished in nature (asiddha).
In principle, this is indeed so. However, the aggregate as a real entity possesses those characteristics; yet because it lacks causal nature, consciousness cannot arise from those characteristics.
Since the aggregate-characteristic consciousness does not arise, and that [aggregate] does not produce this consciousness, how could this [consciousness] take that as its object?
Because the characteristic of the object of cognition is inconsistent, it does not fulfill the definition of an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Because of this, what was previously stated—that their reasoning is consistent—is not established.
This is the correct explanation for why [the opponents] posit an object of cognition (*ālambana*); however, there is no actual sense of "cognizing" it.

That is to say, by means of the various proofs put forward by other vehicles, they fail to realize that all is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). From the perspective of the Mahāyāna, none of these can be established. In reality, this is the case.

Thus, it seems unnecessary to clarify what others commonly accept before refuting it. Nevertheless, when the aggregate of the *ālambana-vijñāna* (object-cognizing consciousness) arises, that aspect (*nimitta*) truly exists;
therefore, one may allow that it possesses the status of an object-condition (*ālambana*).

However, because it is definitively not the nature of the cause, and because that aspect is a mere conceptual synthesis (*prajñapti-saṃghāta*), it cannot produce the five sensory consciousnesses. One should understand this aggregate accordingly.
The consciousness that takes a collection as its characteristic cannot be produced by that conventional aggregate.
Since that conventional aggregate cannot produce this consciousness, how could it cause this consciousness to take that aggregate as its object?
For it is logically impossible for that which cannot produce consciousness to serve as the objective aspect (nimitta) of that consciousness. Therefore, since [the aggregate] does not exist...

The meaning of "condition" (pratyaya) is not the same as the meaning of "object-condition" (ālambana). For this reason, the reasoning regarding their association proposed by the second school mentioned previously is likewise definitively untenable.

If that is so, what is the characteristic of the object-condition (*ālambana-nimitta*)? Whatever is an object must, by principle, give rise to a cognition that resembles its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
That cognition which conforms to the object is the producer; that [object] is the object-condition.

Some say that whatever serves as an object must, by principle, necessarily be the cause for the arising of the mind and mental factors. Once this has arisen, it functions by experiencing [the object] in accordance with that object.

Regarding discourse: at that time, this is designated as the "object-condition" (*ālambana-viṣaya*). If an object possesses these two characteristics, only then can it be properly termed an "object-condition.

It is the nature of being able to produce, which is the nature of being an object-condition. Citing the *Āgama* (i.e., the *Āgama*, here translated as "Teaching"), this is precisely what explains the nature of producing conditions.
Because it is the cause of production, that consciousness arises with it as its condition; this is universally accepted.
The objective realm as it manifests its own essential nature is of no benefit here; therefore, it is not discussed.
This presentation of questions and answers serves to clarify once more the correct meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Question:

If that is so, then since the collective aggregate is neither a productive condition nor an object-condition, what ultimately constitutes the characteristic of an object-condition? Answer: [The response follows].
It is said: "In principle, whatever constitutes an objective referent (*ālambana*) must be able to produce a cognition that possesses a self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) similar to it;
thus, the cognition corresponding to that object takes that very characteristic as its producer and takes that very characteristic as its objective referent.
Furthermore, there is another teaching which states: "In principle, whatever constitutes an objective referent must necessarily be a manifestation of the mind and..."
It is the cause for the arising of the mind. That is to say, once this consciousness has arisen, it experiences the characteristics of its objects and gives rise to verbal expression;
at that time, these are termed "objects of cognition" (*ālambana*). If an object possesses these two characteristics, [it is established as such].
This alone is properly designated as the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya). That is to say: first, it is the nature that is capable of producing consciousness;
second, it is the nature that serves as the object of consciousness. The scriptural teachings cited above precisely describe this nature of being a productive condition.
Because it is the cause of production, it causes that consciousness to arise in relation to its object; only then [is it truly an object-condition].

If it is universally admitted that its own essential nature appears as the object-condition (*ālambana*), how can one then maintain that a "total aggregate" external to the mind serves as the object-condition?
Thus, we know that a total aggregate not only lacks the status of being an object-condition in the sense of being perceived, but also lacks the status of being an object-condition altogether.
However, within this context, their attachment has not yet been entirely refuted; therefore, it is not yet appropriate to set forth the correct measure (*samyak-pramāṇa*) and explain it.
It is useless; therefore, it is not discussed.
That which is a composite aggregate cannot be that which produces [effects], because it is not a real entity. This is because such a composite aggregate is not a real entity.
This is because, within the collection of existents, it is inexpressible as being either identical or different. Furthermore,
there is no unreal entity that possesses the functional capacity to produce an effect, just as a second moon cannot produce the cognition of the appearance of a second moon.
This correctly explains the meaning that [the collection] lacks substantial reality, being like a second moon.
As for why the author of the present treatise is able to refute and reject the claim that the aggregate is the producer:
it is because the aggregate is certainly not a real entity. Since this aggregate is not a real entity, it exists only as a combination of atoms.

Because the two natures of identity and difference cannot be predicated. That is to say, if one were to assert that the aggregate and the atom are identical, then while the aggregate would be visible, the atom would not.

If one were to assert that the aggregate and the atom are different, then apart from the collection of atoms, no separate intrinsic nature of the aggregate could be found. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "A lump of clay and its atoms..."
Dust is neither different nor non-different [from its cause].
Furthermore, there is no unreal thing that can possess the functional capacity to produce an effect. Therefore, the analogy is like a second moon:
just as a second moon cannot actually produce the appearance of a second moon within visual consciousness.
If that is so, for what reason does this appearance arise? It is because the sense faculty is impaired.

When the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is damaged by its clarity being obstructed by cataracts or the like, one perceives two moons arising from the very location of that impaired faculty; this is not because it is a real object.
Although that second moon may appear due to this [condition], it is not the actual object of perception.
This question and answer explain the meaning of the "second moon. A question is asked:
"If it is said that the second moon-image upon consciousness cannot be produced, for what reason does the second moon-image appear to those with cataracts?"
The answer is: This is due to the impairment of the sense faculty.
When the visual faculty has its luminous quality and function damaged by cataracts or other defects, one consequently perceives two moons arising from that impaired faculty.
Since this is not an actually existing object, even if the mental consciousness falsely manifests the appearance of those two moons, they certainly do not [exist as such].

The objective sphere of visual consciousness is like a second moon. Even if this consciousness possesses the appearance of that [object], it is not designated as its object because it does not arise [as such].
This is because, since it lacks the nature of being a real entity and so forth, the aggregate as a whole is not the cause for the arising of consciousness; it lacks the nature of reality.
"It is like a second moon.
This is a reiteration of the preceding meaning, employing an analogy to illustrate the principle.
Fearing that there might be doubt—namely, that since the second moon is seen by the eye, why is it not called the object of visual consciousness?—it is now explained: "It is like a second..."

Candrakīrti: Even if it appears as if that characteristic exists upon this visual consciousness, because it lacks real existence and cannot produce visual consciousness, it is certainly not to be called an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) for visual consciousness. Why is this?
This is because the second moon is not a real entity; it should be understood that the same applies to the aggregate,
as it is not the cause for the arising of visual consciousness, nor is it a real entity, and because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
just like the example of the second moon.
Because it is precisely for this reason that its status as a non-cause is established, it cannot be an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just like a second moon.
Furthermore, by means of this analogy of the second moon, one should understand that the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) is leveled against the theory of mutual causality.
Moreover, because the meaning of consciousness is established through reasoning, such an objection would be contradictory.
That is to say, at the outset, one provisionally grants that there is an object of cognition (*ālambana*), merely negating that which is not an object.

However, once it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that [the object] does not possess the nature of being a cause, then it is likewise not an object of cognition; it is just like the second moon, which is not the objective domain of visual consciousness.

Furthermore, one should understand that this analogy of the second moon is stated to demonstrate the lack of necessary concomitance (*anaikāntika*) regarding the cause characterized by the appearance of an image (*sākāra-hetu*).

This is the fault of consciousness. Furthermore, because the principle that this second moon is merely a false perception of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is established, it reveals that the fault of those who falsely posit a composite whole (*piṇḍa*) as a real entity (*dharmin*) is a contradiction of its own specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha*).

For while other vehicles establish their thesis that a composite whole is the object of cognition (*ālambana*) on the grounds that consciousness carries that image, the Mahāyāna [establishes it differently].

That entity does not exist in reality. To establish the thesis that a composite aggregate is a "non-object-condition" (*ālambana-apratyaya*) constitutes a "common indeterminate fault" (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika-doṣa*) for the other vehicle.
Furthermore, while the other vehicle posits the composite aggregate as a "dharmin" (subject), the Mahāyāna treats the composite aggregate as being like two moons;
how could two moons be established as a *dharmin*? Thus, the other vehicle commits the fault of the "intrinsic characteristic of the subject" (*dharmin-svalakṣaṇa*).
This would contradict the [established] fault.

Furthermore, visual consciousness does not take as its object the atoms of the accumulated blue and so forth, because their substance is not of a nature that arises [as such], just like the consciousnesses of the other sense faculties.
This analogy is commonly accepted, and therefore it is not stated separately.
This is also a separate exposition of the arguments used by certain Mahāyāna proponents to refute the positions of outsiders; it shall not be employed here.
The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: **Thesis:** Eye-consciousness is a subject that does not take as its object a collection of accumulated atoms such as blue.

**Reason:** Because the substance of that collection is entirely a conventional (*prajñapti*) phenomenon and lacks the nature of being a productive cause. **Example:** Like [other conventional phenomena].

The auditory faculty-consciousness and so forth, up to the body-consciousness, are existent phenomena (*dharmas*). [This is] the thesis (*pakṣa*) that they do not take as their object the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the accumulation of tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: "because their substance is not of a nature to arise [from such atoms]. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: "like the visual faculty-consciousness and so forth.

This [reasoning] also contains both the refutation (*apavāda*) and the non-allowance (*anujñā*); fearing that one might not be able to definitively establish that thesis, this present analogy of the two moons is employed.

This clarifies that [the example] is mutually accepted by both parties. If the analogy were applied to other sensory consciousnesses, then the mention of the "object-condition" (ālambana) would become redundant;
therefore, it is not stated separately.
The second analogy of the moon is not a real entity; therefore, it should be understood that this is established as being non-causal.
As it has been said: "Even if the characteristic of having marks exists, it is nonetheless not their condition. This statement further means that it is not their cause.
This correctly elucidates the present second analogy of the moon. It serves merely to demonstrate that [the object] is not a real entity;
one should understand that this is established provisionally as a refutation of the causal nature of the aggregate as a whole. As it is said:

"Even if there is a nature that bears the aspect [of the object], it is not the condition for the arising of that consciousness. This statement further means that it is not the cause for the arising of that consciousness.
First, let us set aside the fault of [the opponent's position] regarding the capacity to produce [an object].
If one says that there is no second moon, how is it that two appearances are currently perceived?

It is because, after internal predispositions (*vāsanā*) have been activated with their specific capacities in a uniform sequence, a consciousness resembling the appearance arises, just as in a dream.

One perceives the arising of an object; by means of this, one falsely forms the understanding that it resembles [a second moon]. Upon that location of the moon, one further observes another through mental projection (*adhyāropa*).
This further dialogue serves to clarify the falsity of the second moon. Internally, the functional capacity is the ultimate eye-faculty (*paramārtha-cakṣur-indriya*).
"Distinction" (*viśeṣa*) refers to impairment. Question: If one says there is no second moon, how [is it so]?
Is it observed that two aspects arise? The answer is:
because there is a distinction in the impairment of the functional capacity for the manifestation of form within the eighth consciousness, two aspects appear where none exist.
Subsequently, the scattered and indistinct mental consciousness arises as if it were those aspects. It is just like perceiving objects when dreaming; by this, [it causes...]
It seems you have formed this erroneous interpretation. While within the sphere of one moon, you ride upon it and further perceive other moons;
how could there ever be such a thing as an external, real object apart from the mind? Alas!

If you understand that two moons are merely manifestations of the mind, then you will know that the entire aggregate of the sense organs, the body, and the physical world is likewise nothing but a manifestation of the mind.
Some say that when two [moons] appear simultaneously to the visual consciousness, because it is difficult to establish a definite sequence between these two, they are taken to be simultaneous;
subsequently, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) then thinks, "I see a second moon.
Others further say that there is a confusion regarding the number of moons as commonly perceived due to the impairment of the sense faculty.
This describes those who do not understand that all is mind-only, and who further give rise to two kinds of false conceptual proliferation regarding the second month.

First, it is said: "When this lunar phase appears simultaneously to the preceding and succeeding moments of that visual consciousness, because it is difficult to definitively establish the sequence of these two, they are taken to be simultaneous; therefore, the preceding and succeeding moments of that visual consciousness..."
Following these two types of appearances, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) then thinks, "I see a second moon. Second, it says:
"It is merely that there is an error in the reckoning of the single moon in the sky, which is commonly acknowledged, due to the impairment of the sense faculty."
There are two types of divergent views.
From the perspective of those schools that do not admit external objects, such various views are merely false attachments.
This is a general refutation of these two positions; below, they will be refuted individually.

Is it not the case that a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), immediately following and induced by what is not an object of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), is able at one time to simultaneously apprehend two forms and thus produce the understanding and perception of seeing two moons?
Furthermore, regarding sounds and so forth, the consciousness that apprehends them does not know their sequence.
Should there not be two sounds and so forth perceived simultaneously? Even for one with keen vision, the successive moments of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are already difficult to discern;
how much more so is it for a consciousness dependent on the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) to discern their distinctions? Thus, many perceptions of dual characteristics and so forth arise.
This refutes the first theory of conceptual proliferation. That is to say:

could these two lunar images possibly be produced by the visual consciousness perceiving them in immediate succession, such that a subsequent distinct mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to simultaneously perceive both images and form this interpretation, thereby thinking it sees two moons?
One should know that the two moons are not only not perceived by the visual consciousness; [they are likewise not produced by it].

Furthermore, it is not the case that the object is the domain of the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Moreover, if one maintains that the two moons are such that the mental consciousness does not know their sequence,
then in the case of sound for the auditory consciousness, odor for the olfactory consciousness, taste for the gustatory consciousness, and touch for the tactile consciousness,
there would likewise have to be two sounds, two odors, two tastes, and so on, because the mental consciousness cognizing them would also not know their sequence.
Do the two perceptions of contact arise simultaneously? Suppose one hears the sound of a single bell and then hears another sound;
even if these occur in successive moments, one certainly does not form the understanding that two sounds are ringing at once.

Why, then, would one specifically form the understanding that two moons appear simultaneously? Furthermore, for a person with healthy vision, the mental consciousness still functions in a sequential manner.
It is difficult to understand; thus, even amidst phenomena that arise and perish moment by moment, one still maintains a view of them as if they were permanent and unitary.
