How much more so for the visual consciousness, which relies upon the physical sense organ—how could it possibly discern the distinctions between preceding and succeeding moments?
Thus, one would end up with the erroneous view that there are two distinct forms and so forth.
If a *caṇḍāla* were to claim that consciousness exists substantially when it has ceased, why would he need to laboriously and falsely superimpose a second moon?
To speak thus regarding numbers involves confusion;
this refutes the second school’s conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). One *caṇḍāla* is simply the single moon in the heavens.
This lunar mansion in the heavens is merely what we all commonly recognize. Apart from cognition (*vijñāna*), how could it ever exist as a reality?
"One month. Since even one month does not exist, why trouble yourself with the false addition of two months? How could you say that there is an error in the number?
Indeed, two months are a false perception arising from individual karma (*bhedakarma*), and one month is likewise a false perception arising from shared karma (*sabhāgakarma*).
Therefore, it is not only the false perception of two months that is called "confusion"; even the false attachment to the existence of a heaven external to the mind is [a form of confusion].
"One" is also a confusion. Since "one" is not real, then "two" cannot be said to have a numerical confusion either.
Treatise: Therefore, regarding the two external factors, each lacks one of the conditions for an object of cognition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); thus, both are logically untenable.
Other vehicles, apart from consciousness, maintain two kinds of grasping—namely, grasping at atoms or grasping at a composite aggregate.

Because these both lack one portion of the [required] meaning, and because they are objects of the power of the refuting reasoning as previously explained regarding the means of proof (*sādhana*), they are established as being inconsistent.
Since each lacks one portion, the manifestation of its own essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) and its capacity to produce [cognition] are necessarily incomplete.
These two parts alone constitute the object of cognition (*ālambana*). At the level of the atom (*paramāṇu*), the first factor is lacking;

at the second extreme [of the whole], the second factor is lost. If this were the case, the two types of faults previously discussed would be gathered back together once more to ensure there is no discrepancy.
The text may be understood accordingly.
Treatise: Some maintain that form and other [sensory objects] each possess many characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), among which one portion is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) mutually support one another, such that each possesses a single characteristic of aggregation (*saṃcita-lakṣaṇa*). This characteristic is substantially existent (*dravyasat*) and is capable of producing [cognition].
Because it appears as if already known, it serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses.

Some say that regarding the characteristic of aggregation (*saṃcita-lakṣaṇa*), each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) possesses its own characteristic of aggregation; it is precisely this aggregated dust that manifests as a characteristic.
According to the number of atoms present, all of these are substantially existent (*dravyasat*). They reside within the locations of the atoms. (That is, each...)

Each [atom] possesses the characteristic of a collective aggregate (saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa). Because the self-characteristic consciousness (svalakṣaṇa-vijñāna) arises [taking that aggregate as its object], and because it exists as a real entity (dravyasat) by virtue of the characteristic of the atom (paramāṇu-lakṣaṇa), it ought to be the objective referent (ālambana).
This is because both factors—the aggregate and the atom—are existent.
This [opponent] further argues that the nature of the atom inherently possesses the characteristic of aggregation (*saṃcita*). This passage is also easy to understand.

The Treatise states: This too is irrational. Why? Because aggregation, like solidity and so forth, even if it serves as a condition for visual consciousness and the other sense-cognitions, is not their object-condition (*ālambana*), since it is admitted to be the characteristic of an atom, just like the characteristic of solidity and so forth.
Although such characteristics are substantially existent (*dravyasat*), [they are not objects].

Regarding visual consciousness and the others, it is possible for them to have external objects as their conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), yet these objects are not their actual objective referents (*ālambana*). This is because the characteristics of those objects do not exist within the visual consciousness and the others.

The same principle should apply to the aggregated characteristics of atoms (*paramāṇu*) such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; for both [the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas] maintain that these are the characteristics of atoms.
This is precisely what was previously established [as being untenable]; [if you] seek further advancement [therein], there is truly no basis for it (I shall now question you):
Is the characteristic of aggregation identical to the atom? Or is it not so? [The proponents of other vehicles reply:

Because the objects of the various domains possess manifold characteristics, each of these atoms possesses its own atomic form and also possesses its own characteristic of aggregation. [I now further challenge: How can this be possible?
How could it be reasonable for two characteristics—the subtle state and the composite—to coexist within a single entity (an atom)?
[The opponent] replies: "In all material things that are gathered together, the nature consists of the four great elements, such as earth and so forth."
They all inherently possess superior capacities (just as earth has the nature of solidity, water the nature of moisture, fire the nature of heat, and wind the nature of motion;

earth can support, water can moisten, fire can transform, and wind can stir). Regarding characteristics such as blue, yellow, red, white, beautiful, or ugly, they function as the five sense objects according to the specific thing [they belong to], and they are apprehended by their respective faculties.
These very atoms, even within their manifold locations, are solid, moist, warm, and mobile; when observed with the eye—

When it is taken by the eye, it becomes visible form; when heard by the ear, it becomes sound; when grasped by the nose, it becomes fragrance; when tasted by the tongue, it becomes flavor; and when perceived by the body, it becomes tangibility.

Even at the location of a single atom (*paramāṇu*), there exists a collective characteristic (*saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa*). Since this characteristic [of the aggregate of atoms] serves as the objective domain for visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions, it possesses the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[Now, a further objection is raised: If this were so, then within each atomic location, the cognition [itself] should also perceive a collective characteristic. Why is this not the case?

Since it has already been stated that objects (*ālambana*) possess a collective aspect (*saṃcita-lakṣaṇa*), why is it not said that the consciousness (*vijñāna*) which takes them as its object likewise possesses that collective aspect?

[This is because the objective part and the subjective part do not share the same substance. To this, the followers of other vehicles reply: "Therefore, it is further stated that within the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the object, there exists a collective aspect."

This very statement serves as a skillful means (*upāya*) to reveal that consciousness (*vijñāna*), as the perceiving subject, also possesses both the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*) and the collective characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

Now, we raise a further objection: If each individual atom possesses this characteristic, then it would already exist prior to the time of aggregation (and thus the characteristic of aggregation would not depend upon gathering).

Why, then, do you speak of a "collective characteristic"? For a mass of form (*rūpa-rāśi*) consists of many [atoms], whereas the infinitesimal atom is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); such is the treatise.

[As for] what is permitted [within this context]: these atoms, because they are of the nature of a collective aggregate, do not exist apart from that aggregate, nor does the aggregate exist apart from the atoms.
Therefore, as previously stated, they are not substantially real; why labor to restate this when there is a further underlying intention?
Even if atoms were substantial entities with distinct individual natures, their characteristics would still not be visible to the eye, but would exist only at the locus of their accumulation.
Since they can be understood through their mutual dependence, one speaks only of the characteristic of aggregation (*saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa*); there is nothing else [to be said].
(How, then, could it be claimed that upon each atom there exists a separate characteristic of aggregation?)
These successive questions are intended to clarify the meaning within the treatise; the text itself is also understandable.
Furthermore, even if all conditioned things (*saṃskāra*) were to exist as individual atoms (*paramāṇu*), having the nature of being aggregated, nevertheless, with respect to a single entity...

The circular and the subtle mutually harmonize and assemble; among them there are degrees of superiority and inferiority (wherein the superior can conceal the inferior). Therefore, for now, we shall observe them according to their respective phenomena. Take, for example, the color blue.

"In this case, the earth element (pṛthivī-dhātu) possesses a superior aggregate of blue color, whereas the atoms (paramāṇu) of the earth element possess inferior characteristics; therefore, one perceives only the blue color and thereby knows the earth element.
Such explanations are indeed consistent with reason.
This is a restatement of the counter-arguments of other vehicles.
Even if one were to grant this, just as when an extremely red object first arises, many factors would be so forceful that there would be no room for [the intended conclusion].
This discussion is conducted based on the possibility of such a case;

it is the correct refutation of this Mahāyāna [position]. That is to say, let us for the moment set aside the fact that there is no green color external to the mind, nor even the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
Even if one were to grant this, when an extremely red object first arises, the red color...
Both are strong; the blue color is also strong. They do not conceal one another.
By this analogy, even if the characteristics of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) and the aggregate (*saṃghāta*) were both strong, there would be no room for the superior to conceal the inferior.
Yet, why is it that we have never seen these two characteristics—the individual minute particle and the aggregate—manifesting simultaneously in a single instance? How could this be possible?
This argument is based on a mere possibility and is ultimately devoid of actual proof.
If that were so, how could it be said that atoms are not seen by the sense faculties?

Furthermore, how could it be maintained that only wisdom can see atoms, given that the characteristics of an object are not the referent of consciousness and are not the objective domain of consciousness dependent upon the sense faculties?
Therefore, it is said that these are not faculties (*indriya*). The meaning of "not being a faculty" is something observed solely by the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*);
this is the refutation by other vehicles and the correct response of the Mahāyāna. The objection states: "If that were so, then when the extremely red [color] first arises..."
The blue cannot be hidden; thus it can be proven that the eye is able to see atoms (*paramāṇu*).
How is it, then, that you followers of the Mahāyāna say that atoms are not the objects of the five sense faculties?

Furthermore, how can you say that only the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), like cognition (*buddhi*), is able to see atoms? Answer: Because the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of an atom is not [an object] of the five [sense faculties].

The meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana*) of consciousness is not the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) of consciousness based on the sense faculties; therefore, it is said to be "non-facultative" (*anindriya*).

This meaning of being non-facultative applies solely to the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which, through the practice of conceptual contemplation (*parikalpita-vidarśanā*), achieves the observation of suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*).
Furthermore, by what reasoning is it that the form of an atom is not perceived when it is actually present, just as its solidity and so forth are not?

Just as with solidity, moisture, and the like, even if such qualities as blue exist within those atoms, they are not the objective domain of visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions, because the capacities of the sense faculties are each restricted to their own specific objects.
It is the same for the atoms; there is no contradiction with what is commonly accepted.
This is also a critique from other vehicles, to which the Mahāyāna provides the answer. "The form of the object" refers to the five sense organs, such as the eye.
The critique asks: By what principle is it established that this appearance of atoms is not perceived by the visual faculty?
The answer is: It is like solidity and so forth; that is to say, just as solidity, moisture, heat, and motion [are not seen] within those colors such as blue and yellow.

Even if such a thing were to exist, it certainly could not be an object of the visual consciousness and the other sensory consciousnesses, because the functions of the sense organs are each restricted to their specific domains.
For example, when the eye perceives blue and so forth, it definitely does not perceive solidity and so forth;

when the body-sense perceives solidity and so forth, it definitely does not perceive blue and so forth. Now, the same applies to atoms: even if they were real, [they would not be perceived by the senses].
Furthermore, it is certainly not seen by the eye, nor is it perceived by the body, and so forth; thus, there is no contradiction with what is commonly accepted.

Is it not the case that the subtle [atoms] lack the nature of solidity because they possess distinct entities? This is asserted in relation to the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), wherein the ten bases (*daśāyatana*) are admitted.
However, the statement that these are "great elements" (mahābhūta) is without fault. This has already been explained.
Yet, this other vehicle (the Śrāvaka-yāna) raises another objection, and the Mahāyāna responds to it. The objection says:

"Since you have used 'solidity' and so forth as metaphors for the aggregation upon the atom (paramāṇu), is this not intended to show that the nature of solidity does not exist upon the atom? Will [you then say]..."

The absence of a solid nature is used to negate the existence of a composite whole; since the exemplifier (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) must necessarily be distinct entities, this still contradicts the meaning commonly accepted [by our school].
[The opponent] replies: This refers to the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) regarding the thesis that [the sense bases] are conditions but not objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, even granting that the ten bases of form—consisting of the internal faculties and external objects—are merely...
It is composed of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). Since it consists of these great elements, how could it be merely a collection [of them] without possessing solidity or moisture?
Therefore, one knows that the analogy and the object of the analogy do not necessarily have separate entities. Thus, these words are free from the fault of contradicting what is commonly accepted.
This has already been stated, and it cannot be challenged by other vehicles.

Treatise: Regarding the position that the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth can take as their objects the various aggregated characteristics of atoms, and that there further arises a distinct cognition of jars, bowls, and the like—according to that position, such distinctions should not exist.
It is not because of a difference in shape that they are distinct, for a difference in shape is not real.
Regarding objects such as jars and bowls, their differences in size and so forth are due to the equality or inequality in the number of atoms that constitute them;

thus, the cognitions apprehending them are likewise without distinction. If it is argued that the cognitions differ because the shapes and physical characteristics of those objects differ, this is also logically untenable.
Distinct shapes, such as the neck [of a jar], exist only in relation to conventional dharmas like jars and do not belong to the atoms themselves.
O you who perceive jars, bowls, and the like: you claim that what is perceived as a composite is the very substance of the atoms themselves.

If this were proven, then with respect to jars and bowls, they would be observed as being identical to the perceptions of the sense faculties (without distinction), because the consciousness regarding their own objects [the atoms] does not deviate.
Furthermore, since sensory perception arises merely in accordance with the presently existing real objects [of the atoms], the consciousness and its object [would be indistinguishable].
Since there is no distinction [between them]—as they are both aggregations of atoms—how can one know the difference between a jar and a bowl?
This verbal designation cannot be made because there is any distinction among the atoms themselves within the locations of the jar, the bowl, and so forth.

Rather, since atoms take as their object a general aggregate at the time of their gathering, it is certainly not the case that they are distinguished when the individual entities of those jars and so forth are being cognized.
Within a collection (saṃcita) of many [atoms], there may be a distinct portion; apart from that, there is no real entity (dravya) as the appearance of those [atoms].
Since no distinct entity of an aggregate can be apprehended, the sense-consciousnesses that take them as objects would necessarily lack any difference in their objective aspects (*nimitta*).
Consequently, because there would be no distinction between [a jar, a bowl, and a fruit], it would follow that the very nature of atoms is what constitutes the objective condition (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, since there is no place where they lack distinct characteristics, one cannot establish a differentiation based on the nature of diverse cognitions upon re-examination, just as in the case of perceiving blue.

[Just as] when [one perceives] blue, it is ultimately blue and one never forms the cognition of yellow, red, or the like; so too, if one were actually perceiving a multitude of atoms such as those of a jar or a bowl, they would likewise remain ultimately nothing but that multitude of atoms, and one should not form a distinct cognition of "jar" or "bowl.

Furthermore, if you claim that because their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ, the designations differ—whereby "characteristics" refers merely to differences in shape and arrangement due to the distinct forms of the neck, belly, base, and so forth of the jar and bowl—then [the cognition] must arise from the distinction of the objects.

This, then, is indeed a distinction that accords with reason. (However, according to your own tenets, since you maintain that atoms are the objects [of cognition], it is absolutely certain that) there is no such thing (as this differentiation).
Why is this? Because there is no differentiation among the atoms within the objective field perceived by the sensory consciousnesses.
Yet this aggregate is merely a *pudgala* (a conventional existence), and this aggregate is certainly not [an object] of the sensory consciousness (as a direct perception).

As for the object (*viṣaya*), this has already been refuted (so why labor to state it again?). Furthermore, it cannot be said that the distinction between objects—which are not [the primary] causes—gives rise to differences in the characteristics of consciousness;
such a view would not be consistent with reason.
This refutes their counter-argument that when cognition arises from a collection [of atoms], it still takes the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) as its objective referent (*ālambana*).

Therefore, they claim that since there is no difference between the atoms of a jar and those of a bowl, the cognition of them should likewise be without distinction; thus, cognitions such as "jar" or "bowl" ought not to exist.
*Kṣaṇika* (kṣīra-ti) is translated as "provisionally existent" (*prajñaptisat*). The rest of the text is self-evident.

(The followers of other vehicles ask: "Furthermore, how is it known that distinct spatial configurations do not exist within atoms? (The Mahāyāna answers: "Because the form and characteristics of atoms have no differentiation.
Generally, for any entity that possesses constituent parts, there must necessarily be distinct configurations that manifest across various spatial locations."
However, the essence of atoms has no spatial dimensions; having reached their ultimate limit, how could they ever possess distinct shapes?

Even though objects such as jars and bowls may differ in their physical manifestations, the nature of their constituent atoms never differs. This is because they are a single substance, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, it is certain that at the level of a composite aggregate, there is no real entity possessing spatial dimensions. Whatever possesses spatial orientation [is not ultimately real].
The arrangement of shapes (belongs to the category of conceptual constructs). None of these are objects of the five sensory consciousnesses (as perceived through direct perception).
Through the many such refutations above, the intention is to demonstrate that there is a distinct characteristic [within consciousness].

One must understand that the cognition of jars, bowls, and so forth, does not take a distinct entity composed of an aggregation of atoms as its objective referent; it is just like the mental states regarding *sukha* and *duḥkha*.
*Sukha* means pleasure; *duḥkha* means suffering. This indicates that pleasure and suffering reside solely within one's own consciousness; how could there be external objects?
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Treatise: One should not maintain that atoms (*paramāṇu*) also possess distinct spatial forms. Why is this? Because the magnitude of atoms is equal;
distinctions of form exist only conventionally (*prajñapti*). When one analyzes [an object] down to its ultimate atoms, the cognition of it is necessarily abandoned;

therefore, jars, bowls, and the like cannot constitute atoms with distinct spatial dimensions. Since the characteristic of the spherical atom is abandoned, one knows that [the distinction] is merely conventional.
Shape is provisional and not real. Furthermore, when shape is separated from its substance and analyzed down to the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), the cognition of it is necessarily abandoned;
however, the cognition of substances such as blue does not cease even when they are analyzed down to the ultimate atoms.

Therefore, shape exists only conventionally and does not exist as a real entity like blue and other colors. Consequently, the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses is not external form and so forth.
This principle is fully established.

However, because atoms are equal in measure, they constitute a non-distinct object; this precisely demonstrates that they do not possess the nature of being objects for the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness.
If one were to say that distinctions in characteristics necessitate distinctions in discourse, the intent of this statement is to clarify that it was not previously claimed they are non-distinct.

Regarding the claim that [atoms] constitute an object (*viṣaya*), this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). The intention of those [of other vehicles] is to say that atoms are the object;

in reality, there is no difference [between our positions]. However, they distinguish them on account of their distinct shapes and characteristics (whereas the Mahāyāna maintains that atoms have no distinction).

We also agree that this is a case of proving what is already established, because there is no difference in the magnitude of atoms. This distinction of shape exists only as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

The manifestation of distinct phenomena constitutes their specific objects (and this does not occur at the level of atoms; therefore, it is a false claim of the Hīnayāna that atoms also possess differentiation). Answer: This has not yet been established.
This correctly clarifies that while one may grant that atoms are without distinction, it is thereby revealed that their distinct shapes are not real.
Alternatively, this may clarify that the consciousnesses of the various sense faculties do not possess the nature of atomic characteristics within objects such as jars or bowls.

It is not an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just as other consciousnesses are. "Other consciousnesses" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) or the sensory consciousnesses (*indriyavijñāna*).

This is because when perceiving blue, there is no appearance of yellow; and although the atoms (*paramāṇu*) are numerous in substance, they lack differentiation [in that specific perception], whereas the sensory consciousnesses possess differentiated appearances.
Thus, it is established that these do not have the nature of being objective particles (*viṣaya-rūpa*).

Alternatively, one may state the syllogism as follows: "The sense-faculties and consciousnesses with respect to jars, bowls, and so forth" is the subject (*dharmin*). "They are not object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*)" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because they lack the nature of the characteristics of atoms (*paramāṇu*). The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is: "Just like other consciousnesses."

Regarding the phrase "other consciousnesses," this refers to the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Generally speaking, the preceding five sensory consciousnesses are established as the objects of comparison (*dṛṣṭānta*), while the mental consciousness serves as the subject of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Alternatively, the various sense-faculty consciousnesses may serve as both the subjects and objects of comparison for one another.
For instance, when visual consciousness perceives only blue, because there is no appearance of yellow, yellow is not an objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for that perception.
Now it is the same here. When perceiving a jar or a bowl, there is no characteristic of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Although the substance of these atoms is manifold, they lack any differentiation;
yet, because the sensory consciousnesses possess differentiated characteristics, how could atoms possibly serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
This establishes that the objective condition is definitively not of the nature of atomic particles. As previously admitted:
Since those atoms are without distinction, the fact that they manifest as distinct shapes proves that they are merely conventional and cannot serve as conditions.

Now, furthermore, by means of the distinctions between the faculties and consciousnesses, it is shown that atoms are not the objects of cognition. This is the subtlety of this method of concession and refutation.
Regarding the verse’s mention of the distinction between atoms (*paramāṇu*), the question and answer are the same as before.

If it is admitted that their collective aggregation (*saṃcita*) conceals their individual characteristics, then the principle that shape (*saṃsthāna*) is not a real object (*dravya*) can be established. Such a superior reasoning ought to be proven.
As asked previously: "Furthermore, how is it known that the distinct forms of the various atoms do not exist? The answer was:
"Because there is no difference in the form and appearance of the atoms. Now, in this verse, the question and answer are the same as before:

if one accepts that when jars and bowls are gathered together as a whole, they are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*) that conceal the characteristics of the atoms, then shape is not a real object.
Only then can the principle be established. Thus, since the atom (*paramāṇu*) is not the object of cognition (*ālambana*), and the aggregate is not substantially real, both attachments are refuted;
it is clearly known that there are no phenomena external to the mind. Such a superior principle ought to be established.

If it is claimed that such things as jars and bowls exist apart from atoms, then—just as when those jars and bowls are analyzed down to their atoms—the cognition of them (the jars and bowls) would immediately cease to exist, just like [the cognition of] an army and so forth.
Therefore, this statement that jars and the like exist is not a real meaning.
Because [the jar and so forth] are not real entities (*avastu*), this demonstrates that the various non-real things asserted by other schools cannot abandon their contradictory natures.
Just as with the word "equal," the cognition of blue does not exist;

this distinct characteristic is a conventional existence (*prajñaptisat*) based on concealment, because it takes the jar and so forth as its objective nature (and is thus certainly analyzable). However, when not yet analyzed, one perceives only the jar and so forth, and does not perceive the atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Once [the pot] has been analyzed, even the characteristic of the pot no longer exists. Thus, since the pot is not real and the atoms are likewise not the objective referent (*ālambana*), although they may cite numerous divergent views and principles, they ultimately fail to demonstrate that the substantial entity of the atom possesses any distinct nature.

This explanation also refers to the passage concerning the analysis of distinct objects down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth. The above concludes the refutation of external form as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Treatise: Is that object-condition entirely non-existent? It is not entirely non-existent. If so, how is it [existent]? Internally...

Visible form appears as if external and serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness. It is accepted that its aspect (*ākāra*) resides within consciousness because it can produce consciousness.
Although external objects do not exist, there is internal form that appears similar to an external object, serving as the objective condition.
This is because it is accepted that visual and other consciousnesses bear that aspect and arise from it; thus, it possesses both of these two criteria.
Based on the nature of internal objects, this refers to establishing the objective referents of one's own school.

If one were to universally deny the existence of objective referents, it would entail the faults of contradicting worldly consensus as well as contradicting one's own accepted tenets; for the four types of conditions are taught in the Mahāyāna sūtras.
This first explains the meaning that it is not entirely non-existent.

Herein, the term "internal" indicates that there is an object of cognition which does not exist apart from consciousness. As for the phrase "the substance of the object (form)," this refers to the apprehended portion;
it signifies the sense that consciousness transforms itself into the appearance of an object. However, [this] is distinguished as being external to consciousness.

[The opponent] maintains that by taking this *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) as the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), one does not contradict their own school; however, the fault of contradicting worldly consensus remains as before.
Since worldly convention universally accepts that objects exist externally, one should now say they are "like external" [objects] in order to avoid contradicting the world.

Nevertheless, this [aspect] is not separate from consciousness; it is merely that the apprehended portion (*grāhyāṃśa*) appears as if external, which the deluded do not realize, and thus they think, "I..."
One perceives external objects and gives rise to the conceit of grasping at them as such; however, in reality, it is solely this internal transformation that serves as the cause.

It is like the appearance of hair and so forth within the visual consciousness (in the empty space)—how could there be actual hair existing outside of consciousness? Although external objects do not exist (yet are falsely imagined by the ignorant), the Mahāyāna now seeks to eliminate the notion that they are real.
There is no external object (as it is grasped), because its nature is not that which is cognized by the sense-consciousnesses.

When investigated through reasoning, it is impossible to claim that its own essence—which is definitely situated externally—is what is cognized (let alone the fact that there is no object external to the mind).

Even if one were to grant that such external forms truly exist, they could not be the objects of cognition, because they do not possess the nature of being the aspect (*ākāra*) of that consciousness. [They are not] in the consciousness...
As previously stated, when the appearance of atoms manifests, how could one take those atoms as the objective referent? Now, necessarily, it is just as when external forms appear.
This is precisely what constitutes the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This explains the meaning of the two phrases: "internal form appearing as if external" and "serving as the objective condition for consciousness.

Regarding the statement that it is "distinctly divided from outside consciousness," consciousness has four parts: the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the verifying-of-self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga*) are called the two internal parts.
The seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) are called the "two external divisions," but this does not mean they exist outside of consciousness.

The rest may be understood accordingly. Regarding the phrase "because it accords with the principle of the image": this [image-division] is precisely that which is transformed by this [consciousness];

just as the nature of a direct cause or condition is never separate from consciousness, so too [the image] accords with the principle of its own image. Furthermore, because it accords with the principle of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it manifests [as] one's own consciousness.

The transformation that arises—namely, the distinct nature and characteristics of the objects of perception—is as stated in such passages as "consciousness possesses those marks," which clarifies that it does not depend upon external things as its objects.
Rather, the objective aspects as conceived by the mind arise concomitantly with it.

Furthermore, regarding what is conceived by the mind (the notion that there is an object external to the mind), in reality, if one were to separate it from consciousness, it would necessarily not exist externally. Therefore, these objective aspects are fundamentally never separate from consciousness.

For this reason, it is called the "internal objective aspect" (antar-jñeya-lakṣaṇa). In this verse, the term "internal" (antara) merely signifies that which is not separate from consciousness (vijñāna).
Since there is fundamentally no object external to that consciousness, in relation to what could it be considered "internal"?
This explanation accepts the principle that the aspect (of the object) resides within consciousness. "In relation to" (*wang*) means "in contrast to" (*dui*). The rest may be understood accordingly.

And because the [perceiving] consciousness arises from this [objective aspect], it is only when this [objective aspect] exists that the [subjective] aspect can arise. Alternatively, the phrase "from this" may be understood as follows:

since the seventh consciousness and the preceding five consciousnesses differ in their functional meaning (the seventh conceives of non-self as self and takes an incorrect object, whereas the preceding five are direct perceptions taking real objects), the consciousness cannot exist apart from its real object;
therefore, only when this [objective aspect as a real object] exists does [the consciousness] then [arise].

Regarding the arising of consciousness (the seventh [type of] object-condition, which carries an object with a substantial basis), its image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) arises from both ends; therefore, it is called "the conjunction of two dharmas. It is not said that the fifth [type of object-condition] is also a conjunction of two dharmas.
This is the explanation of the meaning of "that which can produce consciousness.

It clarifies its two aspects: the object-condition (*ālambana*) and the capacity to produce [consciousness] by carrying a representative image (*nimittabhāga*). Because it accords with reason, it constitutes a valid proof (*sādhana*).

This establishes that [the five consciousnesses] take only the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as their proof, thereby demonstrating that they do not take external objects as their conditions. If one were to distinguish them further:
Regarding this, it is acceptable that the southern [position] does not depend on external objects. Within the context of the dream state, this serves as a demonstration.

As it is said, two factors constitute a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): first, that consciousness possesses the aspect of the object; second, that consciousness arises. It is through these two functions that a single valid cognition is established.
This concludes the establishment of the proof (*sādhana*). It also serves to conclude the intention of not distinguishing [the object] in terms of the sixth consciousness.

"Common characteristic object" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-viṣaya*) refers to the receptacle world, the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), and the ephemeral sense organs (*aupabhogika-indriya*). If it is *jñāna*, this is translated as "wisdom" (*zhi*); if it is *prajñāna*, [it is translated as "discernment"].
This refers specifically to the sixth consciousness. That the objects perceived by the sixth consciousness are not external to the mind can be clearly understood through the analogy of a dream;
therefore, there is no need for further debate.
Treatise: Since these internal objective aspects are not separate from consciousness, how can they arise simultaneously and yet act as conditions for that consciousness?

Furthermore, even granting for the sake of argument that such internal aspects exist, one observes only the illusory appearance of external objects; therefore, it is said that there are no external aspects.

Just as one conceives of an object according to one's own mental projections, a corresponding experience arises; the characteristics of that object appear within [the consciousness], as if in a mirror.
While this might seem reasonable, how can that which is already a part of the consciousness itself serve as the causal condition for the simultaneous arising of that same consciousness?

Since that which constitutes the apprehended portion does not exist apart from consciousness, it is itself a portion of consciousness; yet for it to arise again as consciousness would entail the fallacy of contradicting its own nature.
Furthermore, because it is of the same nature as that [consciousness] (the example), just like the apprehending portion, how could the apprehender give rise to the apprehender?
This would thus result in the impossibility of its being generative by nature. Moreover, if one were to claim that [it arises] merely through external characteristics...

It arises from the defiled consciousness (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*). This means that the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the consciousness arise simultaneously. It cannot be said that these two, though simultaneous, possess the nature of cause and effect (as in the process of mutual production).

How could it be logical for the two horns of an ox to stand in a relationship of one being the cause and the other the effect? Furthermore, this is not possible even when things that are non-different exist at the same time;
they are spoken of together here by using the term "concomitant" (*sahabhū*). Moreover, [the objective aspect] does not exist outside of the consciousness.
Setting aside the discussion of the objective realm, these two are fundamentally not two distinct entities. How, then, can they be called "co-existent" (*sahabhū*)?
This is the objection raised by proponents of other vehicles.
Treatise: Because they are determined to follow one another, they act as conditions simultaneously; or, the preceding acts as a condition for the succeeding by inducing its functional capacity.
This is the actual principle. However, due to the power of their distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are conjectured to be different and thus expressed as such.
Because there is a distinction between the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*), this consciousness is consequently differentiated.
This is the Mahāyāna response.

If it were so, then even the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-svabhāva*) would be merely that which is grasped; the things of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would not possess an intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*).
This would consequently result in the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) being non-genuine;

this is another difficulty for other vehicles. That is to say, if the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) were merely expressed through conjecture, then this nature of the object-condition would also have to be merely the imaginatively constructed (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and could not be called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).
If things possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they would consequently fail to be of a truly dependent nature.
This is not contradictory, for the meaning of "dependence" is likewise accepted by all regarding other distinct objects that are clung to as real.

Just as when consciousnesses of the same class (*sabhāga*) that have ceased in immediate succession (*samanantara-niruddha*) act as a cutting instrument, this [subsequent] consciousness also takes four kinds of manifold conditions (*pratyaya*) as its conditions.

This is the second response and explanation of the Mahāyāna: namely, although the objects of conceptualization (*vikalpa-vastu*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is not contradictory for them to function as such.

Regarding the meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): just as other [schools] maintain that various objects such as empty flowers, illusions, and dreams, though all lacking reality, are merely the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) manifested by one's own mind, and are universally accepted as functioning as object-conditions;
and just as immediately preceding mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), upon ceasing, serve as the prior and subsequent conditions for their own corresponding class of consciousness.

At the moment of severance, although it is not a distinct entity, the preceding consciousness that has just ceased serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the subsequent thought-moment.
One should know that this consciousness likewise functions as a condition by way of four kinds of multiple conditions. These four kinds are the four conditions mentioned in the preceding text;
however, because the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is not of a single type, they are termed "multiple conditions. This should be established.

The *Pramāṇa* states: "The objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the same substance is a dharma that exists; it is established as the thesis (*pakṣa*) that it functions as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: because the common portion (*sabhāga-bhāga*) performs the function of delimitation. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is like the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The above merely explains the meaning of the two phrases: "because they are determined to be concomitant" and "they also act as conditions simultaneously. The remainder has not yet been explained; perhaps the Sanskrit original has not yet arrived.
Alternatively, since the explanation of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) has already been established, it need not be further commented upon.
*The Direct Explanation of the Treatise on the Object-Condition* concludes here.
